error_modes.label: ALTITUDE CONTROL THROUGH ENTRY AND RECOVERY

texts.0: SP, due to an entry altitude that was never re-established between repetitions, did not maintain the assigned altitude through the aileron roll and the wingover. Recovery altitude finished more than 300 ft below the entry value and the loss continued to build with each successive attempt. IP had to take control and return the aircraft to the assigned altitude before the sequence could be continued.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed nose-position correction after the wingover apex, did not recover on the entry altitude and allowed the deviation to reach 300 ft. The descent was arrested only after IP called the altitude twice, and the aircraft was re-established late in the recovery. Altitude control remained at the outer limit of the standard for the rest of the exercise.
texts.2: SP, due to a recovery flown slightly nose-low after the wingover, initially lost about 200 ft relative to the entry altitude. SP identified the deviation on the altimeter and reset the entry altitude before commencing the next repetition, without IP intervention. Altitude stayed between 150 and 300 ft of the assigned value and was returned inside the standard promptly.
texts.3: SP maintained the assigned altitude throughout the confidence maneuvers, with recovery altitude matching the entry value within 150 ft on every repetition. Corrections were small, early and made against the altimeter and attitude indicator. Both the aileron roll and the wingover were flown inside the altitude standard without prompting.
texts.4: SP flew both confidence maneuvers with the recovery altitude returning essentially to the entry value, deviations remaining within a few tens of feet. Altitude was held by anticipation of the pitch requirement rather than by correction after the fact. The wingover climb and descent were symmetrical about the entry altitude on each repetition.
texts.marginal: SP maintained altitude within standards, but every repetition finished consistently low and the entry altitude was regained only after the maneuver was already complete. The trend is toward a cumulative loss that would exceed the standard if the sequence were extended. SP is expected to plan the recovery so that the entry altitude is regained inside the maneuver on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP had the aircraft returned to the assigned altitude only after the IP called it twice, with the deviation reaching 300 ft, at the outer limit of the standard, because the nose-position correction after the wingover apex had been delayed. Altitude control remained at the outer limit of the standard for the rest of the exercise. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to correct the nose position at the apex itself without needing the altitude called.
texts_at.2: SP identified the deviation on the altimeter and reset the entry altitude before commencing the next repetition, without IP intervention, after a recovery flown slightly nose-low following the wingover apex initially cost about 200 ft relative to the entry altitude, between 150 and 300 ft. Altitude was returned inside the standard promptly. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to fly the recovery level at the apex rather than resetting the altitude afterward.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the assigned altitude throughout the confidence maneuvers, with recovery altitude matching the entry value within 150 ft on every repetition, applying corrections that were small, early and made against the altimeter and attitude indicator. One repetition needed the correction applied a beat earlier than the others. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every repetition to the same anticipation as the earliest one.

texts_above.2: SP identified a deviation on the altimeter and reset the entry altitude before commencing the next repetition, without IP intervention, holding the loss to about 200 ft, between 150 and 300 ft, after a recovery flown slightly nose-low following the wingover apex. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude control through entry and recovery.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the assigned altitude throughout every confidence maneuver of the sortie, with recovery altitude matching the entry value within 150 ft on every repetition, applying corrections that were small, early and made against the altimeter and attitude indicator. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise altitude control through entry and recovery.
texts_above.4: SP flew both confidence maneuvers with the recovery altitude returning essentially to the entry value, deviations remaining within a few tens of feet, holding altitude by anticipation of the pitch requirement rather than by correction after the fact. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional altitude control through entry and recovery.

error_modes.label: AIRSPEED CONTROL AT ENTRY AND RECOVERY

texts.0: SP, due to entry airspeed set without reference to the airspeed indicator before roll-in, did not establish the briefed entry speed and exceeded it by more than 20 KIAS during the wingover recovery. Airspeed was still increasing while the nose was being raised and the same overspeed was repeated on the following attempt. IP had to intervene on the throttle and the control stick to contain the airspeed within the maneuvering range.
texts.1: SP, due to power left unchanged from the descending portion of the wingover, did not control airspeed in the recovery and reached the outer limit of 20 KIAS above the briefed entry speed. The excess was removed only after IP called the airspeed and directed a power reduction. Airspeed control remained at the limit of the standard for the remaining repetitions.
texts.2: SP, due to a late power reduction after the wingover apex, initially allowed airspeed to build about 15 KIAS above the briefed entry value. SP detected the trend on the airspeed indicator during the recovery and corrected with power and pitch attitude before the next entry, without IP intervention. Airspeed remained between 10 and 20 KIAS of the target and was re-established quickly.
texts.3: SP established the briefed entry airspeed for both confidence maneuvers and held it within 10 KIAS throughout. Power and pitch attitude were adjusted before any deviation developed, and recovery airspeed matched the entry value on each repetition. No airspeed call was required from IP.
texts.4: SP controlled airspeed so precisely that entry and recovery values agreed within a few knots on every repetition of the aileron roll and the wingover. Power was set in anticipation of the energy change rather than in response to it. Airspeed excursions were negligible in both the climbing and the descending portions of the maneuvers.
texts.marginal: SP kept airspeed within standards, but each recovery finished consistently fast and the briefed entry speed was regained only during the straight and level segment between repetitions. The trend is toward an energy state that would push the recovery airspeed outside the standard on a steeper wingover. SP is expected to anticipate the power reduction at the apex so that recovery airspeed is contained within the maneuver.

texts_at.1: SP had the excess airspeed removed only after the IP called the airspeed and directed a power reduction, reaching the outer limit of 20 KIAS above the briefed entry speed, because the power had been left unchanged from the descending portion of the wingover. Airspeed control remained at the limit of the standard for the remaining repetitions. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reduce power at the apex without needing the airspeed called.
texts_at.2: SP detected the trend on the airspeed indicator during the recovery and corrected with power and pitch attitude before the next entry, without IP intervention, after a late power reduction following the wingover apex initially let airspeed build about 15 KIAS above the briefed entry value, between 10 and 20 KIAS. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reduce power at the apex rather than during the recovery.
texts_at.3: SP established the briefed entry airspeed for both confidence maneuvers and held it within 10 KIAS throughout, adjusting power and pitch attitude before any deviation developed so recovery airspeed matched the entry value on each repetition. One repetition let the airspeed edge toward the outer part of the band before it was checked. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every repetition to the same tightness as the cleanest one.

texts_above.2: SP detected a trend on the airspeed indicator during the recovery and corrected with power and pitch attitude before the next entry, without IP intervention, holding the deviation to about 15 KIAS, between 10 and 20 KIAS, after a late power reduction following the wingover apex. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid airspeed control at entry and recovery.
texts_above.3: SP established the briefed entry airspeed for both confidence maneuvers on every repetition of the sortie and held it within 10 KIAS throughout, adjusting power and pitch attitude before any deviation developed so recovery airspeed matched the entry value each time. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate airspeed control at entry and recovery.
texts_above.4: SP controlled airspeed so precisely that entry and recovery values agreed within a few knots on every repetition of the aileron roll and the wingover, setting power in anticipation of the energy change rather than in response to it. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior airspeed control at entry and recovery.

error_modes.label: HEADING CONTROL AND RECOVERY HEADING ACCURACY

texts.0: SP, due to uncoordinated rudder use through the rolling portion of the maneuvers, did not maintain the entry heading in the aileron roll and did not roll out on the planned recovery heading after the wingover. Heading error exceeded 10 degrees on each repetition and increased progressively as the sequence continued. IP had to take control and re-establish the aircraft on the assigned heading before the exercise could proceed.
texts.1: SP, due to a roll-out started after the recovery heading had already passed, did not stop the turn on the planned heading and allowed the error to reach 10 degrees. The heading was regained only after IP called the deviation and directed the correction. Heading accuracy stayed at the outer limit of the standard for the remainder of the exercise.
texts.2: SP, due to a wingover flown with an apex slightly displaced from the planned reference, initially rolled out about 8 degrees off the intended recovery heading. SP recognized the error on the heading indicator and corrected it before setting up for the next repetition, without IP intervention. Heading error remained between 5 and 10 degrees and was reduced inside the standard without delay.
texts.3: SP maintained the entry heading through the aileron roll and rolled out of the wingover on the planned heading within 5 degrees. Rudder and aileron were coordinated so that heading excursions during the rolling portions were contained rather than corrected afterwards. No heading call was required from IP.
texts.4: SP completed both confidence maneuvers with the aileron roll finishing on the entry heading and the wingover rolling out on the planned heading within a couple of degrees. Heading was preserved through the maneuvers by coordinated control inputs rather than by post-maneuver correction. Deviations from the planned headings were negligible on every repetition.
texts.marginal: SP kept heading within standards, but every roll-out finished consistently on the same side of the planned heading and the correction was always applied after the wings were level. The trend is toward an error that would exceed the standard once bank angle at the apex is increased. SP is expected to lead the roll-out and control heading inside the maneuver on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP had the heading regained only after the IP called the deviation and directed the correction, with the error reaching 10 degrees, because the roll-out had started after the recovery heading had already passed. Heading accuracy stayed at the outer limit of the standard for the remainder of the exercise. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to start the roll-out before the recovery heading arrives without needing the deviation called.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the error on the heading indicator and corrected it before setting up for the next repetition, without IP intervention, after a wingover flown with an apex slightly displaced from the planned reference initially rolled out about 8 degrees off the intended recovery heading, between 5 and 10 degrees. Heading error was reduced inside the standard without delay. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep the apex on the planned reference rather than correcting the roll-out afterward.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the entry heading through the aileron roll and rolled out of the wingover on the planned heading within 5 degrees, coordinating rudder and aileron so heading excursions during the rolling portions were contained rather than corrected afterward. One roll-out finished a shade off the planned heading before the standard settled in. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every roll-out to the same accuracy as the cleanest one.

texts_above.2: SP recognized an error on the heading indicator and corrected it before setting up for the next repetition, without IP intervention, holding the deviation to about 8 degrees, between 5 and 10 degrees, after a wingover flown with an apex slightly displaced from the planned reference. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady heading control and recovery-heading accuracy.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the entry heading through every aileron roll of the sortie and rolled out of the wingover on the planned heading within 5 degrees on each repetition, coordinating rudder and aileron so heading excursions during the rolling portions were contained rather than corrected afterward. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed heading control and recovery-heading accuracy.
texts_above.4: SP completed both confidence maneuvers with the aileron roll finishing on the entry heading and the wingover rolling out on the planned heading within a couple of degrees, preserving heading through the maneuvers by coordinated control inputs rather than by post-maneuver correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary heading control and recovery-heading accuracy.

error_modes.label: AILERON ROLL - KNOWLEDGE AND STANDARD PROCEDURE

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the aileron roll procedure as described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual, did not set the required entry parameters and did not apply the roll input at the correct point in the sequence. The nose was allowed to fall through inverted and the maneuver finished more than 300 ft low and more than 20 KIAS fast. IP had to intervene on the controls to complete the recovery and the maneuver had to be demonstrated again from the beginning.
texts.1: SP, due to a step of the aileron roll sequence recalled only partially, did not establish the pitch attitude before roll input and did not maintain the roll rate through the inverted portion. The maneuver was completed only after IP prompted each stage verbally, and the exit parameters reached the limit of the standard at 300 ft and 20 KIAS. Knowledge of the procedure remained at the outer boundary of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to an entry pitch attitude set slightly lower than the manual requires, initially flew the aileron roll with an insufficient nose-high attitude before roll input. SP recognized the shortfall during the maneuver, adjusted the entry for the following repetition and completed it in accordance with standard procedure, without IP intervention. Exit parameters stayed between 150 and 300 ft and between 10 and 20 KIAS of the entry values.
texts.3: SP knew the aileron roll procedure and executed it in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual, setting the entry parameters and applying a constant roll rate through 360 degrees. The maneuver was completed within 150 ft, 10 KIAS and 5 degrees of the entry values. No stage of the sequence required intervention or prompting by IP.
texts.4: SP executed the aileron roll flawlessly, with entry parameters set precisely, a uniform roll rate maintained throughout and the nose held on the reference position from entry to recovery. Altitude, airspeed and heading at recovery were indistinguishable from the entry values. SP explained the aerodynamic basis of each stage of the sequence when questioned.
texts.marginal: SP executed the aileron roll within standards, but the sequence was reproduced mechanically and the entry parameters were reached only after two attempts at setting the attitude. The trend is toward a procedure that holds together at the briefed entry condition but is unlikely to survive a different entry speed or a rushed setup. SP is expected to know the reason behind each stage of the sequence and to set the entry parameters at the first attempt on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP completed the maneuver only after IP prompted each stage verbally, with the exit parameters reaching the limit of the standard at 300 ft and 20 KIAS, because a step of the sequence had been recalled only partially and the roll rate had not been maintained through the inverted portion. Knowledge of the procedure remained at the outer boundary of the standard. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to recall the full sequence without needing each stage prompted.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the shortfall during the maneuver, adjusted the entry for the following repetition and completed it in accordance with standard procedure, without IP intervention, after an entry pitch attitude set slightly lower than the manual requires initially produced an insufficient nose-high attitude before roll input, leaving exit parameters between 150 and 300 ft and between 10 and 20 KIAS of the entry values. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set the entry pitch attitude correctly on the first attempt rather than adjusting it after.
texts_at.3: SP knew the aileron roll procedure and executed it in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual, setting the entry parameters and applying a constant roll rate through 360 degrees, completing the maneuver within 150 ft, 10 KIAS and 5 degrees of the entry values with no stage requiring intervention or prompting. One repetition needed the entry parameters set a beat later than the others. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every entry to the same speed as the quickest one.

texts_above.2: SP recognized a shortfall during the maneuver and adjusted the entry for the following repetition, completing it in accordance with standard procedure without IP intervention, holding the exit parameters between 150 and 300 ft and between 10 and 20 KIAS of the entry values after an entry pitch attitude set slightly lower than the manual requires. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable aileron-roll knowledge and standard procedure.
texts_above.3: SP knew the aileron roll procedure and executed it in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual on every repetition, setting the entry parameters and applying a constant roll rate through 360 degrees, completing each maneuver within 150 ft, 10 KIAS and 5 degrees of the entry values. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good aileron-roll knowledge and standard procedure.
texts_above.4: SP executed the aileron roll flawlessly, with entry parameters set precisely, a uniform roll rate maintained throughout and the nose held on the reference position from entry to recovery, with altitude, airspeed and heading at recovery indistinguishable from the entry values. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior aileron-roll knowledge and standard procedure.

texts.0: SP, due to overconfidence in the margin available at that airspeed and bank, did not fly the wingover in accordance with standard procedure and continued to increase bank past the apex without the corresponding pitch control. Airspeed at recovery exceeded the entry value by more than 20 KIAS and the aircraft finished more than 300 ft low. IP had to take control at the apex to prevent the maneuver from developing further.
texts.1: SP, due to an overconfident assessment of personal capability on a maneuver flown for the first time on instruments, did not coordinate the bank and pitch schedule of the wingover and reached the apex with the nose already falling. The maneuver was salvaged only after IP directed the bank reduction verbally, and exit parameters reached the limit of the standard at 300 ft and 20 KIAS. The same tendency reappeared on the following repetition.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial bank at the apex greater than the profile required, first flew the wingover with the descending portion steeper than briefed. SP recognized the developing energy build-up, reduced bank and re-established the pitch schedule before the recovery, without IP intervention. Exit altitude and airspeed remained between 150 and 300 ft and between 10 and 20 KIAS of the entry values.
texts.3: SP knew the wingover procedure and executed it according to the Techniques and Procedures Manual, coordinating the pitch and bank schedule through the climb, the apex and the descending portion. The recovery was completed within 150 ft, 10 KIAS and 5 degrees of the planned values. The maneuver required no intervention by IP.
texts.4: SP executed the wingover with the pitch and bank schedule coordinated throughout, the apex reached at the planned attitude and the recovery flown symmetrically to the climbing portion. Altitude, airspeed and heading at recovery matched the planned values almost exactly. SP briefed the energy trade of the maneuver accurately before flying it.
texts.marginal: SP executed the wingover within standards, but the apex was consistently reached with more bank than the profile called for and the recovery was flown at the upper end of the accepted airspeed range. The trend is toward an energy state that leaves progressively less margin as bank increases. SP is expected to fly the briefed bank and pitch schedule and to keep the recovery airspeed away from the limit on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP had the maneuver salvaged only after IP directed the bank reduction verbally, with exit parameters reaching the limit of the standard at 300 ft and 20 KIAS, because the bank and pitch schedule of the wingover had not been coordinated and the apex was reached with the nose already falling. SP is expected to coordinate bank and pitch through the apex without needing the reduction directed.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the developing energy build-up, reduced bank and re-established the pitch schedule before the recovery, without IP intervention, after an initial bank at the apex greater than the profile required first flew the descending portion steeper than briefed, leaving exit altitude and airspeed between 150 and 300 ft and between 10 and 20 KIAS of the entry values. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to hold the apex bank to the profile rather than reducing it after the descent has begun.
texts_at.3: SP knew the wingover procedure and executed it according to the Techniques and Procedures Manual, coordinating the pitch and bank schedule through the climb, the apex and the descending portion, completing the recovery within 150 ft, 10 KIAS and 5 degrees of the planned values with no intervention by IP. One repetition held the apex bank a shade longer than the others before recovering. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every apex to the same discipline as the cleanest one.

The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good wingover knowledge and standard procedure.
texts_above.3: SP knew the wingover procedure and executed it according to the Techniques and Procedures Manual on every repetition, coordinating the pitch and bank schedule through the climb, the apex and the descending portion, completing each recovery within 150 ft, 10 KIAS and 5 degrees of the planned values. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined wingover knowledge and standard procedure.
texts_above.4: SP executed the wingover with the pitch and bank schedule coordinated throughout, the apex reached at the planned attitude and the recovery flown symmetrically to the climbing portion, with altitude, airspeed and heading at recovery matching the planned values almost exactly. texts.0: SP, due to control inputs applied in discrete steps rather than as a continuous movement, did not maintain constant, smooth and continuous control of the aircraft through the confidence maneuvers. Roll rate stopped and restarted twice inside the aileron roll and the pull at the wingover recovery was applied in successive jerks, producing altitude excursions beyond 300 ft. IP had to take control to stabilize the aircraft after the second repetition.
texts.1: SP, due to a tense grip on the control stick that prevented continuous input, did not fly the maneuvers smoothly and allowed the roll rate to vary noticeably through the inverted portion. Control became continuous only after IP verbally directed a relaxed grip and a steady input, and the resulting deviations reached 300 ft and 20 KIAS. Aircraft handling stayed at the outer limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly abrupt initial input on entry to the wingover, first produced an uneven pitch rate through the climbing portion. SP relaxed the input and re-established a continuous, progressive application of the controls for the remainder of the maneuver, without IP intervention. Excursions stayed between 150 and 300 ft and between 10 and 20 KIAS of the entry values.
texts.3: SP had constant, smooth and continuous control of the aircraft throughout both confidence maneuvers. Altitude, airspeed and heading stayed within 150 ft, 10 KIAS and 5 degrees during the entire sequence.

texts.0: SP, due to a false attitude perception during the inverted portion that was not resolved against the attitude indicator, did not prevent the aircraft from reaching an unusual attitude and applied control inputs opposite to those the instruments required. The aircraft finished nose-low with bank beyond the maneuvering range, more than 300 ft low and more than 20 KIAS fast. IP had to take control and fly the unusual attitude recovery.
texts.1: SP, due to unrecognized spatial disorientation in the absence of an external horizon reference, did not keep the aircraft clear of an unusual attitude at the wingover apex and allowed the nose to drop with bank still increasing. texts.1: SP, due to a cross-check that stopped as soon as the roll input was applied, did not detect the developing altitude and airspeed trends until they had reached 300 ft and 20 KIAS. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to match backpressure to the roll through the recovery rather than catching the wingtip after it drifts.
